title: Electric current as a flow of charge

learning_outcomes.text: understand that an electric current is a flow of charge carriers

external_knowledge: SI quantities describe measurable physical properties.

prior_knowledge_summary: AS Topic 1 quantities and units, including SI base units, derived units and unit conversions.
new_learning: Electric current requires moving charge carriers, whose identity depends on the conducting material.
Current compares how rapidly charge passes a chosen cross-section.

blocks.heading: The lamp lights, but what crossed the wire?
content: A metal wire is already full of electrons before it is connected. When a lamp lights, did new electrons race all the way from the cell, or did charged particles already inside the wire begin to move?
Predict what must cross an imaginary line through the wire for there to be an electric current.

figure.purpose: Create the need to distinguish energy transfer from the motion of charge carriers.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show a simple cell, switch and lamp joined by a wire. Add one enlarged cutaway of the wire filled with small electron dots and an unlabeled imaginary cross-section. Do not show current equations.
figure.alt_text: A simple lamp circuit includes a magnified metal wire containing many electrons and an imaginary cross-section.

blocks.heading: Current needs charge and movement
content: Choose an imaginary cross-section through a conductor. If charged particles pass through that cross-section, charge is flowing. That flow is electric current.

A stationary charged particle carries charge, but it does not create a current through the cross-section. An uncharged moving object also does not create electric current. Both charge and motion across the section are needed.

figure.purpose: Separate the two necessary ideas: a carrier must be charged and must cross the section.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Use a two-by-two comparison: charged and moving, charged and stationary, uncharged and moving, uncharged and stationary. Highlight only charged and moving as producing charge flow across a vertical line.
figure.alt_text: Four cases compare charged or uncharged particles that are moving or stationary across a line.

blocks.heading: The definition to learn
content: Definition to learn: electric current is the rate of flow of charge.

The word rate matters. A greater current means charge passes the chosen cross-section more rapidly. This lesson uses that meaning in words. The equation connecting charge, current and time comes in Lesson 2.

figure.purpose: Make the meaning of rate visible without introducing the later Q = It equation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show two equal time windows beside two wire cross-sections. In the first, a small amount of charge crosses; in the second, a larger amount crosses. Label only smaller current and larger current.
figure.alt_text: Two wire cross-sections show different amounts of charge crossing in the same time, representing smaller and larger currents.

blocks.heading: Follow the carriers in a metal
content: Inside a metal, positive ions are fixed in a lattice. Some electrons are free to move through the metal. These mobile electrons are the charge carriers.

Imagine watching one cross-section for the same short interval in two wires. More electronic charge crosses the second section, so the second wire has the greater current. We do not need to count individual electrons or use an equation yet.
Check the model: if all free electrons stopped crossing the section, no charge would flow through it and the current there would be zero.

figure.purpose: Teach the metal carrier model and distinguish fixed ions from mobile electrons.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Draw a magnified metal lattice with large fixed positive ion circles and small mobile electron dots. Show several electrons crossing a dashed section between two snapshots. Use short labels fixed ions and mobile electrons.
figure.alt_text: A metal lattice contains fixed positive ions and mobile electrons crossing a dashed section.

blocks.heading: Different conductors use different carriers
content: A current is not always a flow of electrons alone. In an electrolyte, positive and negative ions can move through the liquid. In an ionised gas, ions and electrons can both carry charge.
The shared rule is deeper than the material: identify the charged particles that can move, then ask whether they cross the chosen section. Those moving charged particles are the charge carriers.

figure.purpose: Compare carrier identities across three conducting materials.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Create three side-by-side cutaways: metal with mobile electrons, electrolyte with positive and negative ions, ionised gas with ions and electrons. Use different simple marker colours and arrows, with fixed lattice ions clearly not moving.
figure.alt_text: Metal, electrolyte and ionised gas cutaways show their different mobile charge carriers.

blocks.heading: Charge carriers are not used up by a component
content: It can feel as if a lamp consumes electrons because the lamp needs a current to work. That picture confuses moving charge with transferred energy.

Charge carriers enter and leave the component. They are not steadily destroyed inside it. A component can transfer energy while charge continues through the conducting path. Later lessons will quantify charge flow and energy transfer separately.

figure.purpose: Repair the belief that a lamp consumes charge carriers.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show before and after counts of electron dots entering and leaving a lamp segment over matching time windows. Use a separate small energy arrow leaving as light and heating, but avoid potential difference or power labels.
figure.alt_text: Equal amounts of electronic charge enter and leave a lamp segment while energy leaves as light and heating.

blocks.heading: A three-question carrier check
content: For any current, ask three questions. What particles are charged? Which of them are free to move? Do they cross the section being considered?

Then state the central idea precisely: electric current is the rate of flow of charge. In a metal the moving carriers are electrons; in an electrolyte they are ions; in an ionised gas they can be ions and electrons.
Do not yet calculate charge, count elementary charges or use drift speed. Those methods are built in Lessons 2 and 3.

figure.purpose: Summarise the transferable carrier-identification method and lesson boundary.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Draw a three-step flow chart: charged, mobile, crosses section, then identify current. Add three tiny material icons with electron, ion, and mixed carrier labels. Do not include formulas.
figure.alt_text: A flow chart identifies charged mobile particles crossing a section, with examples for three materials.

concepts_taught: electric current requires moving charge carriers
current compares the rate at which charge passes a cross-section
carrier identity depends on the conducting material
misconceptions_addressed: Any moving particle produces electric current.
Electric current in every material is carried only by electrons.
next_lesson_can_assume: The exact definition of electric current as rate of flow of charge.
Electric current is a flow of mobile charge carriers.
Electrons carry current in metals, while ions carry current in electrolytes.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Use of Q = It or Q = Ne.
Use of I = Anvq or drift speed.
